# Introduction {.unnumbered} :::: {.callout-warning collapse='false' appearance='minimal'} ## [Caution]{style='font-weight: bold; font-size: 1.10em;'} ::: {style='font-size: 1.05em; color: #282b2d;'} This section is still being developed. The contents are subject to change. ::: :::: ## `ggplot2` syntax > “*making infinite use of finite means*” (Wilhelm von Humboldt) Every language has rules for what words mean and how to order them.[^grammar] R is a language for working with data, and `ggplot2` follows R’s rules: * a thing that holds data is like a **naming** word, and * the set of steps that does something to that thing is like a **doing** word[^nouns-verbs] A graph is a picture of data that we make with code. `ggplot2` graphs are built one layer at a time. A layer is one part of a graph that we put on top of the parts under it. We can start with a few layers and keep adding more until the graph is just what we want.[^layers] ### The Data Layer The data layer is a table, like a page of numbers on a computer.[^rectangular] A column is one list of values that runs down a table, and a row is one line across it. Every set of data in this book is made up,[^simulated] so we’ll make one here: 150 home computers sold in 1998, with the company that made each computer (`brand`), the system it runs (`os`), how fast it works (`cpu_mhz`), and its price (`price_usd`).[^pc-columns] Faster computers cost more, and newer systems add a little to the price.[^win98] ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(1998) pc_sales <- tibble( brand = sample(c("Compaq", "Dell", "Gateway"), 150, replace = TRUE), os = sample(c("Windows 95", "Windows 98"), 150, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.4, 0.6)), cpu_mhz = sample(c(133, 166, 200, 233, 266, 300, 350, 400), 150, replace = TRUE), price_usd = round(700 + 4 * cpu_mhz + if_else(os == "Windows 98", 150, 0) + rnorm(150, 0, 200))) ggplot(data = pc_sales) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](intro_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-1-1.png){width=576} ::: ::: ### The Mapping Layer The mapping layer joins columns in the data to things we can see in the graph, such as how far across and how far up each point goes. An axis is a number line along one side of a graph.[^aes] ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(data = pc_sales, mapping = aes( x = cpu_mhz, y = price_usd ) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](intro_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-2-1.png){width=576} ::: ::: **Plan 1**: data, mapping, and one way to show the data[^template] ```r ggplot(data = ) + geom_*(mapping = aes()) ``` ### The Stats/Geoms Layer The `geom_*()` parts of the code pick how to show the data in the graph: as points, lines, bars, and more.[^geoms] They can also work out new numbers from the data before they show it,[^stat] and move things so they don't cover each other.[^position] ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(data = pc_sales, mapping = aes( x = cpu_mhz, y = price_usd ) ) + geom_point( aes( shape = brand, color = os ) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](intro_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){width=576} ::: ::: We can put many layers (data, mapping, and ways to show the data) in one graph. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(data = pc_sales, # layer 1 mapping = aes( x = cpu_mhz, y = price_usd ) ) + geom_point( aes( shape = brand, color = os ) ) + # layer 2 geom_smooth( mapping = aes( x = cpu_mhz, y = price_usd), se = FALSE ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](intro_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){width=576} ::: ::: **Plan 2**: Plan 1 + a second way to show the data[^template-1] ``` r ggplot(data = ) + geom_*(mapping = aes()) + geom_*(mapping = aes()) ``` ### Position, Labels & Themes With a set number of things and steps, we can put the rules of `ggplot2` together to make graphs without end.[^infinite] ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(data = pc_sales, # layer 1 mapping = aes( x = cpu_mhz, y = price_usd ) ) + geom_point( aes( color = os ) ) + # layer 2 geom_smooth( mapping = aes( x = cpu_mhz, y = price_usd), se = FALSE ) + # layer 3 facet_wrap( . ~ brand, ncol = 2 ) + # labels labs( x = 'Processor speed (MHz)', y = 'Price (USD)', title = 'Home PCs in 1998', subtitle = 'Faster processors cost more', caption = 'Simulated data', color = 'Operating system' ) + # themes theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.box = "vertical") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](intro_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){width=576} ::: ::: **Plan 3**: Plan 2 + small graphs, a new look, and words[^template-2] ```r ggplot(data = ) + geom_*(mapping = aes()) + geom_*(mapping = aes()) + facet_* + theme() + labs() ``` ## Graph Categories Each graph in this book is in one of the groups below (you can see them in the list of parts on the left side of the page). - **Univariate**: graphs of one column[^univariate] - **Amounts**: how many, or a few simple numbers that stand for one or two columns[^amounts] - **Proportions**: how the parts of something make up the whole[^proportions] - **Distributions**: where the values in one column fall, and the form they take[^distributions] - **Dates & Times**: how numbers or groups change over time (by day, month, year, and so on)[^dates] - **Relationships**: how a change in the values of `x` goes with a change in the values of `y` (and sometimes `z`) Some graphs could fit in more than one group. Where that's true, I've tried to add links in the notes to the other places they fit. ## Assumptions I've tried to write code that you can read and understand without running it.[^intro-1] Still, the examples expect you to be able to look inside things in R and answer questions about how they're built.[^skimr-inspectdf] [^skimr-inspectdf]: If not, I highly recommend the [`skimr`](https://docs.ropensci.org/skimr/) and [`inspectdf`](https://alastairrushworth.github.io/inspectdf/) packages for getting to know your data better. ## Style & structure Each graph has the parts below: 1. **Theme** - *The look we give every graph on the page: its colors, its letters, and the old thing it takes them from.* 2. **Requirements** - *What this graph needs, and a first look at it.* 3. **Description** - *A short note on where the graph comes from, what it's for, and what we see in it.* 4. **Set up** - Packages - *Code to get the newest form of the code we use, when we need it.*[^dev] - Data - *The code that makes up the data for the graph (with `set.seed()`, so you get the same values every time).* 5. **Distribution** - *How the rule we used to make up the data gives the graph its form, in three steps:*[^dist-steps] - ***COUNT IT***: *look at a few values and a few numbers that stand for all of them.* - ***DRAW IT***: *show the data as a bar model or as a graph with notes on it.* - ***NAME IT***: *write down the rule and show what each number in it does to the graph.*[^name-it] 6. **Grammar** - Graph Code - *The words around the graph start with `labs_`* - *The graph layers start with `ggp2_`* 7. **More info** - Other ways to make the graph, other choices, and other uses[^more-info] - *Sets of colors*\ - *Other code that works well with it* The picture below shows how the parts fit together. We make up the data in **Set up**, talk about it in **Distribution**, and turn it into a graph in **Grammar**. ```{mermaid} %%| fig-align: 'center' %%| fig-cap: 'The sections in each graph chapter' %%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': { 'fontFamily': 'monospace', 'fontSize': '14px', 'darkMode': false}}}%% flowchart TD thm(["Theme
colors + letters"]) --> req(["Requirements
what the graph needs"]) --> desc["Description
what the graph shows"] desc --> setup[/"Set up
packages + simulated data"/] setup --> dist subgraph dist["Distribution"] count["i. COUNT IT
values + summaries"] --> draw["ii. DRAW IT
bar model or
annotated graph"] draw --> name["iii. NAME IT
distribution +
parameters"] end dist --> grammar[["Grammar
labs_* + ggp2_*"]] grammar --> more(["More info
other geoms + options"]) style thm fill:#4CBB9D,color:#FFFFFF,rx:5,ry:5 style req fill:#4CBB9D,color:#FFFFFF,rx:5,ry:5 style desc fill:#FFFFFF,color:#000000,stroke:#333 style setup fill:#C0C0C0,color:#000000,stroke:#333 style dist fill:#FFFFFF,color:#000000,stroke:#333,stroke-width:1px,rx:10,ry:10 style count fill:#000080,color:#FFFFFF,rx:5,ry:5 style draw fill:#000080,color:#FFFFFF,rx:5,ry:5 style name fill:#000080,color:#FFFFFF,rx:5,ry:5 style grammar fill:#FFFFFF,color:#000000,stroke:#333 style more fill:#4CBB9D,color:#FFFFFF,rx:5,ry:5 ``` I've tried to keep things short and clear, but when I have to pick one, I pick clear. I've also followed a general rule: if one of the `geom_*` steps in `ggplot2` can build a graph easily, I show that way first. The first part of the book starts with bar graphs, which show how many times each group shows up in one column. [^intro-1]: This field manual follows [The Rule of Least Power](https://www.w3.org/2001/tag/doc/leastPower.html), in the sense that "*a language with a straightforward syntax may be easier to analyze than an otherwise equivalent one with more complex structure.*" [^grammar]: Grammar is the system of rules for a language (word meanings, internal structure, and word order). Syntax is the form, structure, and order used to build statements. [^nouns-verbs]: Objects are like nouns, and functions are like verbs (functions "do things" to objects). [^layers]: Layers work like templates we can use to build increasingly customized and complex graphs. [^rectangular]: A rectangular object (like a spreadsheet) with columns and rows. [^simulated]: Simulated. [^pc-columns]: `os` is the operating system (Windows 95 or Windows 98), and `cpu_mhz` is the processor speed in megahertz. [^win98]: Windows 98 adds $150 to the price compared with Windows 95. [^aes]: The mapping layer assigns columns (variables) to visual properties, or aesthetics, with `aes()`. Here `cpu_mhz` goes on the `x` axis and `price_usd` goes on the `y` axis. [^template]: Basic template: data, aesthetic mappings, and a geom. [^geoms]: Geoms (geometric objects), like `geom_point()`, `geom_line()`, and `geom_bar()`. [^stat]: Statistical transformations, like counting values for a bar graph or fitting a smooth line. [^position]: Position adjustments, like stacking or dodging bars. [^template-1]: Template + 1 layer: more geoms and more aesthetic mappings. [^infinite]: With a finite number of objects and functions, we can combine the grammar and syntax of `ggplot2` to create an infinite number of graphs (see the quote above). [^template-2]: Template + 2 layers + facets + theme + labels. `facet_wrap()` splits the graph into small panels (one per `brand`), `theme()` changes the look (here, where the legend goes), and `labs()` adds the labels. [^univariate]: A single variable. [^amounts]: Counts or simple summary statistics. [^proportions]: Part to whole ratios. [^distributions]: The shape of a variable's values (normality, skewness, kurtosis, etc.). [^dates]: Changes in quantitative or categorical variables over a time dimension (date-time, date, year, month, quarter, etc.). [^dev]: Installing development versions of packages (if necessary). [^dist-steps]: How the distribution we simulated from shapes the graph. [^name-it]: Write down the distribution and connect each parameter to the graph. [^more-info]: Additional methods, arguments, or applications.
